minoan-civilization.name: Minoan civilization
minoan-civilization.summary: A Bronze Age culture centered on Crete from about 3100 BC, often called Europe's first civilization, known for monumental palaces, trade and undeciphered writing systems.

linear-b.name: Linear B
linear-b.summary: A syllabic script for Mycenaean Greek, the earliest known form of Greek, dating from around 1450 BC and deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris.

knossos.name: Knossos
knossos.summary: An archaeological site in Crete occupied from the Neolithic period, widely considered Europe's oldest city and the largest centre of the Minoan civilisation; its Palace of Minos was first built around 1900 BC.

cycladic-art.name: Cycladic art
cycladic-art.summary: Art of the Cycladic culture in the Aegean, roughly 3300 to 1100 BCE, best known for simple marble 'folded-arm' figurines, one of three major Bronze Age Aegean art traditions.

minoan-art.name: Minoan art
minoan-art.summary: Art of the Bronze Age Minoan civilization (about 3000–1100 BC), known especially for pottery, frescoed palace architecture, jewellery and carved seals.

bull-leaping.name: Bull-leaping
bull-leaping.summary: Ritual sport of leaping over the back of a charging bull, rooted in Minoan civilization and widely depicted in Bronze Age Minoan art.

phaistos.name: Phaistos
phaistos.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological site in south-central Crete, one of the largest Minoan cities and known for the remains of a Minoan palace.

malia-crete.name: Malia, Crete
malia-crete.summary: Coastal town in Crete, Greece, home to Minoan palace ruins comparable to those at Knossos and Phaistos.

helladic-chronology.name: Helladic period
helladic-chronology.summary: A relative dating system for Bronze Age mainland Greece, about 3200 to 1050 BC, based on pottery styles, paralleling the Minoan scheme used for Crete.

warrior-vase.name: Warrior Vase
warrior-vase.summary: A Mycenaean pottery krater found by Heinrich Schliemann at Mycenae, dated to the 13th or 12th century BC and decorated with a frieze of armed warriors; among the best-known pieces of Late Helladic pottery.

aegean-art.name: Aegean art
aegean-art.summary: Art created around and within the Aegean Sea during the Bronze Age (2800–1100 BC), encompassing Cycladic, Minoan, and Mycenaean styles.

hydria.name: Hydria
hydria.summary: A type of Greek water-carrying pottery vessel made from the 7th century BCE onward, often decorated with mythological scenes.

charles-thomas-newton.name: Charles Thomas Newton
charles-thomas-newton.summary: British archaeologist (1816–1894) who was knighted and made a Knight Commander of the Bath in 1887.

carl-blegen.name: Carl Blegen
carl-blegen.summary: American archaeologist (1887–1971) who directed the University of Cincinnati's excavations at Troy from 1932 to 1938 and also worked at Pylos in Greece.

arthur-evans.name: Arthur Evans
arthur-evans.summary: A British archaeologist (1851–1941) who excavated the Minoan palace of Knossos on Crete and was the first to define the Linear A and Linear B scripts.

late-bronze-age-collapse.name: Late Bronze Age collapse
late-bronze-age-collapse.summary: A sudden societal collapse across the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East in the late 13th to early 12th century BC, ending major Bronze Age powers like the Hittite Empire.

mycenaean-greece.name: Mycenaean Greece
mycenaean-greece.summary: A late Bronze Age Greek civilization, lasting roughly 1750 to 1050 BC, marked by palatial states, art, and the Linear B writing system.

mycenae.name: Mycenae
mycenae.summary: An archaeological site in Greece that was a major military stronghold and centre of Greek civilization in the second millennium BC, giving its name to the Mycenaean period.

pylos.name: Pylos
pylos.summary: A town in Messenia, Greece, inhabited since Neolithic times and a major Mycenaean kingdom, later the site of the Battle of Pylos in 425 BC during the Peloponnesian War.

tiryns.name: Tiryns
tiryns.summary: A Mycenaean hill fort in Greece, one of the most important centers of the Mycenaean world around 1400 to 1200 BCE, known for its massive Cyclopean walls and links to the myths of Heracles.

midea-greece.name: Midea
midea-greece.summary: A Bronze Age citadel site in the Peloponnese, one of the centers of power of Mycenaean Greece alongside Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns.

attu-ili-iii.name: Ḫattušili III
attu-ili-iii.summary: King of the Hittite New Kingdom empire around 1275 to 1245 BC.

achaeans-homer.name: Ahhiyawa
achaeans-homer.summary: A term in Hittite and Egyptian Late Bronze Age texts believed to refer to the Mycenaean civilization, linguistically related to Homer's name "Achaeans" for the Greeks.

great-king.name: Great King
great-king.summary: A historical royal title, used in many languages, marking a monarch as having elevated status above other kings and princes.

greek-dark-ages.name: Greek Dark Ages
greek-dark-ages.summary: A period from about 1180 to 800 BC marked by the collapse of Mycenaean civilization, part of the wider Late Bronze Age collapse across the Eastern Mediterranean.

attarsiya.name: Attarsiya
attarsiya.summary: Mycenaean Greek warlord active around 1400 BC, known from a single Hittite text describing his campaigns in western Anatolia, the earliest record of Mycenaean involvement there.

madduwatta.name: Madduwatta
madduwatta.summary: Late Bronze Age warlord who conquered part of southwest Anatolia, known from the Hittite text called the Indictment of Madduwatta.

atreus.name: Atreus
atreus.summary: Legendary king of Mycenae, son of Pelops and father of Agamemnon and Menelaus, who with his brother seized the throne after their father exiled them for murder.

sea-peoples.name: Sea Peoples
sea-peoples.summary: A group of tribes who raided Egypt and other eastern Mediterranean regions around 1200 BC, once seen as a main cause of the Bronze Age collapse but now often viewed as refugees fleeing an ongoing crisis.

arzawa.name: Arzawa
arzawa.summary: A Bronze Age kingdom and confederation of states in western Anatolia with shifting ties to the Hittites, briefly recognized by Egypt as an independent power before being conquered around 1300 BC.

agamemnon.name: Agamemnon
agamemnon.summary: A mythical king of Mycenae who led the Achaeans in the Trojan War; he was killed on his return home by his wife Clytemnestra or her lover.

arcadia-region.name: Arcadia
arcadia-region.summary: A region in the central Peloponnese, Greece, named for the mythological Arcas and considered in myth the home of Hermes and Pan; later idealized in European Renaissance art.

catalogue-of-ships.name: Catalogue of Ships
catalogue-of-ships.summary: A section of Homer's Iliad listing the leaders, homelands and ship numbers of the Greek forces that sailed to Troy.

linear-a.name: Linear A
linear-a.summary: An undeciphered writing system used by the Minoans of Crete from about 1800 to 1450 BC, the main script of Minoan palace and religious records.

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Ancient Greek poet, possibly born around the 8th century BC, traditionally credited as author of the Iliad and the Odyssey, foundational works of Greek literature.

archaic-greece.name: Archaic period (Greece)
archaic-greece.summary: The period in Greek history from about 800 to 480 BC, marked by rapid population growth, the rise of city-states, the Greek alphabet and early literature.

mycenaean-greek.name: Mycenaean Greek
mycenaean-greek.summary: The earliest attested form of the Greek language, written in the Linear B script and spoken in Mycenaean Greece from the 16th to 12th centuries BC.

kydonia.name: Kydonia
kydonia.summary: Ancient city at the site of present-day Chania in Crete, known from Minoan-era remains and literary sources; added as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025.

archilochus.name: Archilochus
archilochus.summary: Greek poet from Paros (c. 680–645 BC), celebrated for his innovative use of poetic meter and the earliest known Greek author to write mainly about his own feelings.

homeric-greek.name: Homeric Greek
homeric-greek.summary: A literary dialect of Ancient Greek, mainly archaic Ionic with some Aeolic features, used in the Iliad, the Odyssey and the Homeric Hymns.

ionic-greek.name: Ionic Greek
ionic-greek.summary: An ancient Greek dialect spoken in Euboea, the Cyclades and Ionia, used for early Greek poetry by Homer and Hesiod before being replaced by Attic by the late 5th century BCE.

aeolic-greek.name: Aeolic Greek
aeolic-greek.summary: A dialect of Ancient Greek spoken in Boeotia, Thessaly, Lesbos, and Aeolis, known as the language of the poets Sappho and Alcaeus.

attic-greek.name: Attic Greek
attic-greek.summary: The ancient Greek dialect of Athens and Attica, often called Classical Greek, the prestige form taught to students and the basis of later Koine Greek.

thutmose-iii.name: Thutmose III
thutmose-iii.summary: Pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty who ruled from 1479 to 1425 BCE, led 17 to 20 victorious military campaigns, and created Egypt's first navy, earning him the nickname "the Napoleon of Egypt."

argos-peloponnese.name: Argos
argos-peloponnese.summary: One of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, in the Peloponnese region of Greece, and the historic home of the mythical Argive dynasty.

hesiod.name: Hesiod
hesiod.summary: Ancient Greek poet active around 750–650 BC, a near-contemporary of Homer, whose surviving works Theogony and Works and Days are major sources on Greek mythology, farming and early cosmology.

theogony.name: Theogony
theogony.summary: A poem by Hesiod, composed around 730–700 BC, describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods; one of the most important sources for early Greek cosmology.

works-and-days.name: Works and Days
works-and-days.summary: A didactic poem by the Greek poet Hesiod, written around 700 BC, mixing a farmer's almanac with moral advice and myths such as Prometheus and Pandora.

aegean-civilization.name: Aegean Bronze Age
aegean-civilization.summary: The Bronze Age period of the Aegean civilizations, beginning around 3200 BC and encompassing the Minoan, Cycladic, and Mycenaean cultures.

milos.name: Milos
milos.summary: A volcanic Greek island in the Cyclades, source of famous sculptures including the Venus de Milo, with a population of about 5,193 as of 2021.

akrotiri-santorini.name: Akrotiri, Santorini
akrotiri-santorini.summary: A village on the Greek island of Santorini, near an important Minoan Bronze Age archaeological site, one of the most significant of its kind in the Aegean.

pannonian-basin.name: Pannonian/Carpathian Basin
pannonian-basin.summary: A large lowland region in southeastern Central Europe, also called the Carpathian Basin, that formed the core of the historical Kingdom of Hungary and was a settlement zone for migrating steppe peoples.

southern-ural.name: Southern Ural
southern-ural.summary: The wide southern stretch of the Ural Mountains, running from the Ufa River to the Ural River between the East European and West Siberian plains.

shaft-tomb.name: Shaft tomb
shaft-tomb.summary: A deep rectangular burial structure with a pebble floor, rubble-masonry walls and a wooden-plank roof.

therasia.name: Therasia
therasia.summary: A small Greek island in the Santorini group, separated from Thera by the Thera eruption; it had 249 inhabitants at the 2021 census.

santorini.name: Santorini
santorini.summary: A Greek volcanic island in the southern Aegean, also called Thira, shaped by a massive eruption about 3,600 years ago that left its distinctive caldera.

ferdinand-andr-fouqu.name: Ferdinand André Fouqué
ferdinand-andr-fouqu.summary: French geologist and petrologist (1828–1904) who pioneered modern petrographical methods in France and studied volcanic rocks, including on Santorini.

iolcus.name: Iolcus
iolcus.summary: An ancient city, now a small village and municipal unit of Volos in Thessaly, Greece, located north of the Pagasitic Gulf.

thebes-greece.name: Thebes
thebes-greece.summary: An ancient and modern city in Boeotia, Central Greece; once the leading city-state of the Boeotian League, later destroyed by Alexander the Great in 335 BC.

cyclades.name: Cyclades
cyclades.summary: Archipelago in the Aegean Sea southeast of mainland Greece, including the sacred island of Delos and the largest island, Naxos.

amenhotep-iii.name: Amenhotep III
amenhotep-iii.summary: Ninth pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, ruling around 1386–1349 BC during a peak of Egyptian wealth and influence; father of Akhenaten.

nafplio.name: Nafplio
nafplio.summary: A coastal Greek city in the Peloponnese founded in antiquity, later a medieval seaport and the first capital of the modern Greek state from 1827 to 1834.

piyama-radu.name: Piyama-Radu
piyama-radu.summary: A 13th-century BC warlord allied with the Ahhiyawa who led uprisings against the Hittite Empire in western Anatolia, possibly linked to the region behind the Trojan War myth.

dionysus.name: Dionysus
dionysus.summary: Greek god of wine-making, festivity, ecstatic ritual and theatre, whose followers believed they became possessed by him; his origins are uncertain, possibly Mycenaean.

horns-of-consecration.name: Horns of Consecration
horns-of-consecration.summary: A symbol common in Minoan civilization representing the horns of a sacred bull, placed on buildings, tombs and shrines and appearing on seals and painted coffins.

labrys.name: Labrys
labrys.summary: A double-bitted axe that was a sacred symbol of Minoan religion on Crete, later adopted by other ancient religions and modern movements.

temenos.name: Temenos
temenos.summary: An ancient Greek term for land set apart for a king or chief, or dedicated to a god as a sacred sanctuary offering protection to those inside.

mount-ida-crete.name: Mount Ida
mount-ida-crete.summary: The highest mountain on Crete, sacred to the Titaness Rhea and said in myth to be Zeus's birthplace.

rhea-mythology.name: Rhea
rhea-mythology.summary: A Titan of Greek mythology, sister and wife of Cronus, who saved her youngest son Zeus from being swallowed by hiding him and giving Cronus a stone instead.

psychro-cave.name: Psychro Cave
psychro-cave.summary: A Minoan sacred cave on Crete's Lasithi plateau; some legends place the birth of the god Zeus there, though scholars generally reject its identification with the mythical Dikte.

john-chadwick.name: John Chadwick
john-chadwick.summary: English linguist and classical scholar (1920–1998), known for deciphering Linear B together with Michael Ventris.

proto-greek-language.name: Proto-Greek language
proto-greek-language.summary: The Indo-European language ancestral to all Greek dialects, spoken by people entering Greece during the Bronze Age around 2200 to 1900 BC.

anemospilia.name: Anemospilia
anemospilia.summary: The archaeological site of an ancient Minoan temple on Crete.

mount-juktas.name: Mount Juktas
mount-juktas.summary: Mountain in central Crete near Knossos, site of an important Minoan peak sanctuary and possible evidence of human sacrifice nearby.

fournou-korifi.name: Fournou Korifi
fournou-korifi.summary: The archaeological site of a Minoan settlement in southern Crete, one of the places linked to possible evidence of human sacrifice.

thomas-g-palaima.name: Thomas G. Palaima
thomas-g-palaima.summary: A Mycenologist born in 1951, professor and founding director of the Program in Aegean Scripts and Prehistory at the University of Texas at Austin.

peter-warren-archaeologist.name: Peter Warren
peter-warren-archaeologist.summary: British archaeologist, born 1938, specializing in the Aegean Bronze Age and a former professor at the University of Bristol.

minoan-chronology.name: Late Minoan IB
minoan-chronology.summary: A phase within the dating framework used for Minoan civilization, based on pottery styles and palace building phases, since an absolute chronology has proved hard to fix.

megaron.name: Megaron
megaron.summary: The great hall of early Mycenaean and Greek palaces: a rectangular room with a central hearth and columned portico, used for royal functions and court meetings.

cist.name: Cist grave
cist.summary: A small stone-built, coffin-like box used to hold the dead in ancient burials, found across Europe and the Middle East, sometimes grouped under a cairn.
